# 4. Data

<!--

- Describe your datasets and their sources (must be from the approved list).
- Explain variables and data structure.
- Apply the random subset requirement to **both of your datasets**:
  - Use set.seed(your_student_number) (or one group member’s number).
  - Select at least 80% of rows but not the full dataset.
  - Each subset must be used in all further analysis.
- You must also join your two datasets on a common key.
  - It is up to you whether you perform the join before or after subsetting.

-->

Two datasets were obtained from the World Bank's World Development Indicators database.

**Dataset 1: GDP per capita (current US$)**  
Source: https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.CD

This dataset measures gross domestic product per person in current US dollars. It includes country names, country codes, indicator information, and annual GDP per capita values from 1960 to 2025.

**Dataset 2: Life expectancy at birth, total (years)**  
Source: https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.LE00.IN

This dataset estimates the number of years a newborn would live if current mortality patterns remained unchanged. It contains the same geographical identifiers and annual reporting structure.

Both datasets contain 266 country, economy, and regional aggregate records. They share the Country Code variable and reporting years, allowing them to be merged after reshaping into long format.

The datasets are initially presented in wide format, with individual years stored as separate columns. This structure will be addressed during the tidying stage.

```{r data-import}
# Example (replace with your datasets and ID):
# Example of subsetting two datasets
# subset_data1 <- data1[sample(nrow(data1), size = 0.8*nrow(data1)), ]
# subset_data2 <- data2[sample(nrow(data2), size = 0.8*nrow(data2)), ]

# Import the World Bank datasets
gdp_raw <- read_csv(
  "API_NY.GDP.PCAP.CD_DS2_en_csv_v2_1529.csv",
  skip = 4,
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

life_raw <- read_csv(
  "API_SP.DYN.LE00.IN_DS2_en_csv_v2_1528.csv",
  skip = 4,
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Check the dimensions of both datasets
dim(gdp_raw)
dim(life_raw)

# Preview the identifying variables
head(gdp_raw[, 1:4])
head(life_raw[, 1:4])
```
We used `read_csv()` from the readr package to import both World Bank datasets into R. The `skip = 4` argument was applied to exclude the preliminary metadata lines. We then used `dim()` to examine the dimensions of each dataset and `head()` to preview the first six observations.

The results showed that both datasets contain 266 observations and 71 variables. The preview confirmed that the datasets were imported successfully and contain matching geographical identifiers, including Country Name and Country Code. These identifiers will support the subsequent merging process.

```{r data-sampling}
# Randomly sample 95% of rows from each original dataset
set.seed(4280335)

gdp_sample <- gdp_raw[
  sample(nrow(gdp_raw), size = floor(0.95 * nrow(gdp_raw))),
]

life_sample <- life_raw[
  sample(nrow(life_raw), size = floor(0.95 * nrow(life_raw))),
]

# Verify sampled dimensions
dim(gdp_sample)
dim(life_sample)
```

We used `set.seed(4280335)` to ensure that the random sampling process is reproducible. We then applied `sample()` to independently select approximately 95% of the observations from each original dataset, using `floor()` to obtain a whole-number sample size.

The results showed that both datasets were reduced from 266 to 252 observations, while retaining all 71 variables. This corresponds to approximately 94.74% of the original observations, satisfying the requirement to randomly sample at least 80% but less than 100% of each dataset. All subsequent preprocessing steps will use these sampled datasets.

```{r data-tidying}
# Convert GDP dataset from wide to long format
gdp_tidy <- gdp_sample %>%
  select(`Country Name`, `Country Code`, matches("^[0-9]{4}$")) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^[0-9]{4}$"),
    names_to = "Year",
    values_to = "GDP_per_capita"
  ) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year)) %>%
  rename(
    Country_Name = `Country Name`,
    Country_Code = `Country Code`
  )

# Convert life expectancy dataset from wide to long format
life_tidy <- life_sample %>%
  select(`Country Name`, `Country Code`, matches("^[0-9]{4}$")) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^[0-9]{4}$"),
    names_to = "Year",
    values_to = "Life_expectancy"
  ) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year)) %>%
  rename(
    Country_Name = `Country Name`,
    Country_Code = `Country Code`
  )

# Check the dimensions after tidying
dim(gdp_tidy)
dim(life_tidy)

# Preview the tidied datasets
head(gdp_tidy)
head(life_tidy)
```
We used `pivot_longer()` from the tidyr package to reshape both datasets from wide to long format, as the original datasets stored individual years as separate columns. The year columns were converted into a single Year variable, while the corresponding values were stored in GDP_per_capita and Life_expectancy.

We then used `as.integer()` to convert Year from character to integer and `rename()` to standardise the country identifier names. All available years from 1960 to 2025 were retained to preserve the historical observations and allow missing values to be investigated during the scanning stage.

The results showed that both datasets were reshaped into 16,632 observations and four variables. Each row now represents one geographical record in a specific year, making the datasets suitable for merging using Country_Code and Year.

```{r data-merge}
# Check for duplicate country-year keys
sum(duplicated(gdp_tidy[c("Country_Code", "Year")]))
sum(duplicated(life_tidy[c("Country_Code", "Year")]))

# Merge both datasets using Country Code and Year
merged_data <- inner_join(
  gdp_tidy,
  life_tidy %>%
    select(Country_Code, Year, Life_expectancy),
  by = c("Country_Code", "Year")
)

# Check the merged dataset
dim(merged_data)
head(merged_data)
```
We used `duplicated()` to check whether the combination of Country_Code and Year uniquely identifies observations in each dataset. The results returned zero duplicates for both datasets, confirming that each country-year combination is unique.

We then applied `inner_join()` from the dplyr package to merge the two datasets using Country_Code and Year. An inner join was selected to retain only the country-year combinations present in both randomly sampled datasets. We also used `select()` to avoid duplicating the country name variable.

The resulting dataset contains 15,708 observations and five variables, representing 238 geographical records across 66 years (1960–2025). We used `dim()` and `head()` to verify the merged structure and confirm that GDP per capita and life expectancy were correctly combined.


```{r data-filter-countries}
# Import the World Bank country metadata
country_metadata <- read_csv(
  "Metadata_Country_API_NY.GDP.PCAP.CD_DS2_en_csv_v2_1529.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  select(`Country Code`, Region, IncomeGroup) %>%
  rename(Country_Code = `Country Code`)

# Check metadata structure and missing Region values
dim(country_metadata)
sum(is.na(country_metadata$Region))
sum(duplicated(country_metadata$Country_Code))

# Attach country information to the merged dataset
merged_with_metadata <- merged_data %>%
  left_join(country_metadata, by = "Country_Code")

# Keep individual countries and economies only
country_data <- merged_with_metadata %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region))

# Verify the country-level dataset
dim(country_data)
n_distinct(country_data$Country_Code)
head(country_data)
```
We used the accompanying World Bank country metadata as supporting information to identify individual countries and economies and distinguish them from regional aggregates. The metadata contains 265 records, including 48 with missing Region values, and no duplicate country codes.

We then applied `left_join()` to attach Region and IncomeGroup classifications to the merged dataset. These classifications were used to identify the geographical categories of existing observations rather than introduce additional economic or health measurements. Since regional aggregates represent groups of countries rather than individual economies, we used `filter(!is.na(Region))` to exclude them and maintain a consistent country-level analysis.

The results showed that 44 regional and other aggregate records were excluded from the 238 matched geographical records. The resulting dataset contains 12,804 observations and seven variables, representing 194 individual countries and economies across 66 years (1960–2025).

Importantly, the metadata did not modify, replace, or recalculate any GDP per capita or life expectancy values for the retained observations. It was used only to provide country classifications and support the exclusion of aggregates. Therefore, the analysis remains based on the two original World Bank indicator datasets, and their missing values were preserved for investigation during the scanning stage.


# 5. Understand

<!--

- Summarise data structures and variable types.  
- Apply conversions (e.g., character → factor/date, numeric → factor).  
- Ensure your merged dataset meets the minimum criteria:  
  - At least 1 numeric variable  
  - At least 1 character variable  
  - At least 1 factor variable

-->

```{r understand}
# Examine the dimensions and structure of the merged dataset
dim(country_data)
str(country_data)

# Check the class of each variable
sapply(country_data, class)

# Examine the categorical variables
unique(country_data$Region)
unique(country_data$IncomeGroup)

# Check the frequency of income groups
table(country_data$IncomeGroup, useNA = "ifany")
```

We used `dim()` and `str()` to examine the dimensions and structure of the country-level dataset. The results showed that the dataset is stored as a tibble containing 12,804 observations and seven variables.

We then used `sapply()` with `class()` to identify the data type of each variable. Country_Name, Country_Code, Region, and IncomeGroup were classified as character variables, Year as integer, and GDP_per_capita and Life_expectancy as numeric.

We also used `unique()` to examine the categorical values, identifying seven geographical regions and four income groups. The frequency table showed that high-income economies accounted for the largest number of country-year observations (5,016), while low-income economies accounted for the smallest (1,518).

Based on these results, Region and IncomeGroup were identified as suitable variables for factor conversion.

```{r data-conversion}
# Convert Region to an unordered factor
# Convert IncomeGroup to an ordered and labelled factor
country_data <- country_data %>%
  mutate(
    Region = factor(Region),
    IncomeGroup = factor(
      IncomeGroup,
      levels = c(
        "Low income",
        "Lower middle income",
        "Upper middle income",
        "High income"
      ),
      labels = c(
        "Low income",
        "Lower-middle income",
        "Upper-middle income",
        "High income"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

# Verify the data types after conversion
sapply(country_data, class)

# Check factor levels and their ordering
levels(country_data$Region)
levels(country_data$IncomeGroup)
is.ordered(country_data$IncomeGroup)

# Verify income group frequencies
table(country_data$IncomeGroup)
```
We used `factor()` to convert Region from character to an unordered factor because geographical regions are categorical variables without a natural ranking. We also converted IncomeGroup into an ordered factor using four levels, ranging from Low income to High income. The `labels` argument was used to provide consistent and readable category names.

We then used `sapply()` with `class()` to verify the conversions and `levels()` to examine the factor categories. The results confirmed that Region was successfully converted into a factor, while IncomeGroup was classified as an ordered factor. The `is.ordered()` function also returned TRUE, confirming the intended ordering.

The frequency table showed that the original income-group counts remained unchanged after conversion. The dataset continues to contain character, numeric, integer, and factor variables, satisfying the required variety of data types.

# 6. Tidy & Manipulate Data I

<!--

- Identify and explain why your dataset is untidy.  
- Reshape to tidy format using R code.  
- Show before/after structures and explain clearly.

-->
Both World Bank datasets were originally presented in wide format, with each country or economy occupying one row and annual measurements from 1960 to 2025 stored in separate columns.

This structure is untidy for country-year analysis because the year values are embedded in column names rather than stored in a single variable. To satisfy the tidy data principles, each year should be represented as a value in one Year column, with the corresponding GDP per capita or life expectancy measurement stored in another column.

We therefore used `pivot_longer()` in Section 4 to reshape both sampled datasets into long format before merging them.

```{r tidy1}
# Show the original wide format (three example years)
head(
  gdp_sample[, c("Country Name", "Country Code",
                 "1960", "1961", "1962")],
  3
)

head(
  life_sample[, c("Country Name", "Country Code",
                  "1960", "1961", "1962")],
  3
)

# Show the tidy long format
head(gdp_tidy, 6)
head(life_tidy, 6)

# Verify dimensions after reshaping
dim(gdp_tidy)
dim(life_tidy)
```
We used `head()` to compare the structure of both datasets before and after tidying. The original samples contained 252 geographical records and 71 variables, with annual measurements stored in separate columns such as 1960, 1961, and 1962.

After applying `pivot_longer()`, the results showed that both datasets contained 16,632 observations and four variables. The Year column now stores reporting years as integer values, while GDP_per_capita and Life_expectancy contain their corresponding numeric measurements.

The reshaped datasets satisfy the three tidy data principles: each variable occupies one column, each country-year observation occupies one row, and each cell contains a single value. Missing indicator values were preserved for further investigation during the scanning stage.

This structure also allows the two datasets to be merged consistently using Country_Code and Year.

# 7. Tidy & Manipulate Data II

<!--

- Create/mutate at least one new variable from your existing variables.  
- Explain why you created it.

-->

```{r tidy2}
# Create an ordered life expectancy group
country_data <- country_data %>%
  mutate(
    Life_Expectancy_Group = cut(
      Life_expectancy,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 60, 70, 80, Inf),
      labels = c("Below 60", "60-69", "70-79", "80+"),
      right = FALSE,
      ordered_result = TRUE
    )
  )

# Preview the new variable
head(
  country_data %>%
    select(Country_Name, Year, Life_expectancy,
           Life_Expectancy_Group),
  10
)

# Check the structure and levels
str(country_data$Life_Expectancy_Group)
levels(country_data$Life_Expectancy_Group)

# Check the frequency of each group, including missing values
table(country_data$Life_Expectancy_Group, useNA = "ifany")

# Verify the updated dimensions
dim(country_data)
```
We used `mutate()` and `cut()` to create a new variable called Life_Expectancy_Group from the existing Life_expectancy variable. The measurements were classified into four categories: Below 60, 60–69, 70–79, and 80+ years. These categories were created to simplify comparisons of life expectancy across countries and years.

We set `right = FALSE` to ensure that boundary values were included in the appropriate categories and `ordered_result = TRUE` to create an ordered factor. The original Life_expectancy measurements were preserved.

The results showed that the 70–79 group contained the largest number of observations (4,549), while the 80+ group contained the smallest (797). There were also 228 missing classifications, corresponding to missing life expectancy values. The dataset retained all 12,804 observations and now contains eight variables.
